extracted.intended_audience: general readers, parents, industry professionals and policymakers seeking an overview of what 'family-friendly' means
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate whether a product, service, event, or media item is appropriate for all members of an average family, considering cultural values, ratings systems, marketing, amenities, and age/consumption policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: General definition of family-friendly
rubrics_metrics.description: A family-friendly product or service is one that is generally considered by a culture to be suitable for all members of an average family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suitability is culturally dependent; what one culture or family considers acceptable for all ages may differ from another. Use cultural norms as a baseline but expect variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid marketing solely to children; palatable to adults
rubrics_metrics.description: Family-friendly products frequently avoid marketing solely to children and attempt to make the product palatable to adults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing family-friendliness, consider whether features, branding, and messaging appeal across age groups rather than targeting only children. A product that caters to both children and adults scores higher on this dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family-friendly restaurants: service for families with young children
rubrics_metrics.description: Family-friendly restaurants are ones that provide service to families that have young children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate seating, menu options (child-friendly and adult options), facilities (high chairs, changing tables), policies (kids eat/stay free promotions), and staff training to accommodate families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace/political family-friendly policies
rubrics_metrics.description: In politics, new workplace legislation may be introduced to strengthen the family unit through giving parents more flexible family-friendly working hours or educational reforms to helping children with special needs and to give parents more control over how they are schooled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess policies by whether they provide flexible hours, parental leave, special-need education supports, and parental control over schooling—i.e., concrete measures that enable family caregiving and involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospitality: child-focused amenities and segmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hotels and hospitality providers may concentrate services into narrower concepts such as child-friendliness (where children stay and eat free) within the overall family-friendliness customer oriented concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure family-friendliness by presence of child amenities, pricing/offerings (e.g., kids stay/eat free), programming for families, and whether services are deliberately segmented (child-friendly vs pet-friendly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Media content suitability (acceptability for children)
rubrics_metrics.description: The precise definition of 'family-friendly' can vary depending upon the perceived acceptability of content for children (examples include toilet humor, profanity, graphic violence, sexual images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging media, evaluate categories such as crude humor (toilet humor), profanity, violence, and sexual content; also consider how different consumer advocacy groups and parental coalitions view such content. Note that perceptions vary by family values and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family values and ideological influences on perceived suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: The values of the individual family, such as their belief in religion, can also affect whether the family perceives a product as family-friendly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for ideological, religious, and cultural differences: a single media/product may be family-friendly for some families and not for others. Policies or labels should be understood as guidance rather than absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Film and television ratings as indicators (MPAA/TV ratings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the MPAA film rating system and most television content rating systems have ratings for family-friendliness: a G rating in either is universally acceptable for all audiences, while a PG rating suggests that, while generally safe for children to watch, there should be a parent or guardian present for guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use official ratings (G, PG, etc.) as standardized indicators of likely suitability; understand limitations and controversies (e.g., tolerant adults may view higher-rated films as acceptable, and ratings systems have been criticized and debated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Video game ratings (ESRB E rating)
rubrics_metrics.description: The North American Entertainment Software Rating Board, which rates video games, classifies family-friendly content with an E rating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing games, an ESRB E rating is the standard marker for content suitable for general audiences; check descriptors for specific content (e.g., mild language, non-graphic violence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Events/all-ages shows: age restrictions and alcohol policies
rubrics_metrics.description: A family-friendly (or all-ages) show, event or venue refers to one with no age restrictions for entry; minors are permitted to attend live performances. In some cases shows have either no alcohol sales or sales are restricted (wristbands/marks) so underage patrons cannot consume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate events by admission age policy, whether minors can attend, whether alcohol is sold and how sales are restricted, and whether any wristband/marking systems are used. Note: 'All Ages' describes entry policy and does not necessarily indicate thematic or lyrical content restrictions.
